pages.title: The split-phase motor
pages.for: Running a small, easy-to-start load on one phase. A thin-wire start winding puts a second current out of step with the main one, so the field turns. A centrifugal switch drops it out at about 75% speed.
pages.rule:
Main and start windings 90 electrical degrees apart, in parallel on one phase.
Start winding: thin wire, fewer turns. More R, less L, so its current lags less.
Currents about 30° apart: a weak turning field.
Starting torque goes with main current × start current × sine of the angle between them.

Starting torque about 100 to 175% of rated. Starting current high: use the maker's figure.
The switch opens at about 75 to 80% speed and closes again as it slows.
Windings in parallel read lower than either alone.
Example: 4.5 Ω and 15 Ω windings read 4.5 × 15 ÷ 19.5 = 3.46 Ω together.

traps.text: Hums and will not start, yet runs once turning: the start circuit is open. Check the switch and the start winding.
traps.cite: [^15] [^16] Red Seal study guide; Lessons in Electric Circuits

traps.text: The start winding is short-time rated. Frequent or slow starts can burn it out, and so can a switch stuck closed.
It is not momentum that keeps it running. Once turning, the main winding alone makes torque.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead first. A self-resetting thermal cut-out can restart it at any time.
Reverse it by swapping the start winding's leads. Swapping the supply leads does not reverse it.
traps.cite: [^14] [^22] Red Seal study guide; Utah ECE 3600

pages.where: Small fans, pumps and other easy-starting loads, usually up to about 250 W. Not in explosive atmospheres: the switch arcs.

pages.name: How it works
pages.text:
One winding on one phase makes a field that only pulses. It grows, collapses and reverses along one line. At rest, that gives the rotor no push either way.

So a start winding sits 90 electrical degrees round from the main winding, in parallel with it. It is thin wire with fewer turns. That gives more resistance and less inductance, so its current lags the supply less.

The two currents peak at different moments, and the field turns. At about 75% speed a centrifugal switch drops the start winding out.
pages.alt: Main winding: thicker wire, more turns main one pole pair drawn Start winding: thin wire, fewer turns start rotor 90° 230 V, 50 Hz main centrifugal switch closed at rest start

pages.name: The turning field
pages.text: Once started, both windings are fed. Their currents peak 30.1° apart, so the field's tip traces an ellipse and goes round. The rotor runs up. At 1125 rpm the switch opens and the torque drops a step, from 190% to 110%. The windings' field now only pulses, but the rotor keeps turning on the main winding and settles at 1440 rpm. With the start winding wound like the main, both currents lag 50.2°. The field only pulses, and the motor hums at rest.

The two currents peak 30.1° apart, so the field turns and pulls the rotor round. Torque rated, 100% Start winding heat too hot Assume a 230 V, 50 Hz, four-pole motor. Its field turns at 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 rpm. The switch opens at 75% of that, 1125 rpm. On its fan it runs at 1440 rpm.
pages.html:
Then wind the start winding like the main, and try each switch fault.

Assume a 230 V, 50 Hz, four-pole motor. Its field turns at 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 rpm. The switch opens at 75% of that, 1125 rpm. On its fan it runs at 1440 rpm. The field's tip turns only while the two currents are out of step.

Spin the rotor is for the picture only: never spin a live motor by hand.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: Why is the start winding wound with thin wire and fewer turns?
pages.answer: So its current lags the supply less than the main winding's
pages.alt: More resistance and less inductance give a smaller angle in the impedance triangle. Take example windings. Main: 15 Ω resistance, 18 Ω reactance. Arctan(18 ÷ 15) = 50.2° behind. Start: 36 Ω and 13.2 Ω. Arctan(13.2 ÷ 36) = 20.1° behind. That 30.1° gap is what makes the field turn. Wound like the main, both lag 50.2°, and the field only pulses.
options: So its current lags the supply less than the main winding's
So it can stay in and help the motor run
To give it more inductance, so its current lags more
pages.html: More resistance and less inductance give a smaller angle in the impedance triangle. Take example windings. Main: 15 Ω resistance, 18 Ω reactance. Arctan(18 ÷ 15) = 50.2° behind. Start: 36 Ω and 13.2 Ω. Arctan(13.2 ÷ 36) = 20.1° behind. That 30.1° gap is what makes the field turn. Wound like the main, both lag 50.2°, and the field only pulses.

pages.name: How it behaves
pages.text:
Starting torque: low, typically 100 to 175% of rated. It goes with both currents and the sine of the angle between them. Sin 30° is 0.5, against 1 at 90°.

Starting current: high, 5 to 10 times rated. Use the maker's figure.

The switch: opens at about 75 to 80% of full speed, and closes again as it slows.

Running: on the main winding alone, just below synchronous speed. A pulsing field acts like two equal fields turning opposite ways. Once the rotor turns, the one going its way pulls harder.
pages.alt: 0 100 200 0 500 1000 1500 Torque, % of rated Example curve, not a maker's Speed, rpm both windings switch opens main winding only fan load runs here, 1440 rpm

pages.name: Where it is used
pages.text:
Used for: fans, small pumps and other loads that are easy to start, usually up to about 250 W.

Start winding: short-time rated. Frequent starts, or a slow start on a heavy load, overheat it.

Hard-to-start loads: too little starting torque. A capacitor-start motor handles those.

Explosive atmospheres: never use a centrifugal switch there, or inside a sealed compressor. Its arcing can ignite gas.
pages.alt: fan, easy to start split-phase motor

pages.name: Faults and tests
pages.text:
Safety: isolate, lock off and prove dead. A self-resetting thermal cut-out can restart it at any time.

Start circuit open: the switch stuck open, or the start winding burnt open. It hums, will not start, then trips.

Switch stuck closed: it starts, but the start winding stays in. It overheats and can burn out. The overload may trip first.

Resistance: the two windings read in parallel, so lower than either. Reading the main winding alone? The start circuit is open.

Wrong direction: swap the start winding's leads, not the supply.

pages.name: Find the fault
pages.task: A small fan's split-phase motor hums and will not start. After a few seconds its overload trips. The operator says it ran once when he pushed the blades round. What is the likely fault?
pages.alt: With no start current the field only pulses, so it cannot start from rest. Once pushed round, the main winding alone carries it. Never start one by hand. Isolate it, then test the start winding and the switch.
options: The centrifugal switch is stuck closed
